Start building immediately and let the model's general capability handle whatever 'intent' turns out to mean
Pick the largest model so intent understanding is as strong as possible regardless of scope
Write the system prompt first and derive requirements from what it ends up doing
questions.explanation: Vague business language must become checkable functional requirements before design starts. Building first, oversizing the model, or reverse-engineering requirements from a prompt all skip the step that makes the system buildable and testable.

questions.question: A Claude feature has shipped and is live. Which activity belongs to the operate-and-maintain phase of the life cycle, not an earlier phase?
options: Monitoring production quality and cost, and triaging regressions as the model or usage pattern shifts
Writing the initial functional requirements
Selecting which model tier to prototype with
Designing the eval suite for the first release
questions.explanation: Operate-and-maintain is about post-launch monitoring and response to drift or regressions. Requirements, tier selection, and eval design happen earlier, during design and build.

questions.question: The same feature must work inside claude.ai, through the API, and inside Claude Code. A teammate assumes one well-written prompt will behave identically everywhere. What's the flaw?
options: Each surface wraps the prompt in different default context and instruction placement, so identical wording can still behave differently across them
There is no flaw; a single prompt is guaranteed to behave identically across every interface
Only the API supports system prompts
Claude Code ignores system prompts entirely
questions.explanation: Different interfaces layer different default context and instruction handling around the same words, so behaviour can diverge. The API does support system prompts and Claude Code does not ignore them, and no interface guarantees identical behaviour by default.

questions.question: A plugin your app depends on requires plugin B at version 2.x, but you've pinned plugin B at 1.x elsewhere in the project. What kind of problem is this?
options: A plugin dependency conflict that must be resolved by aligning versions or isolating the plugins before either can be trusted in production
A harmless duplication, since plugins do not share state and version numbers are cosmetic
A pure performance issue that only affects load time
Something only the model can resolve at runtime by picking whichever version seems newer
questions.explanation: Conflicting version requirements across plugins is a dependency conflict that needs explicit resolution, exactly like any software dependency graph. It is not cosmetic, not purely a performance concern, and not something the model silently arbitrates.

questions.question: Your app pins claude-model-2026-06-15 in production. A new dated version is released with a documented breaking change to how it formats numbered lists. Which TWO are correct next steps?
options: Test the new version against your eval suite and downstream parser before promoting it
Read the release notes for the specific breaking change and check whether your prompt or parser depends on the old formatting
Upgrade immediately in production, since a dated release is always safe to adopt without testing
Ignore the release notes since breaking changes only apply to floating aliases, not dated versions
questions.explanation: A documented breaking change demands checking your specific dependency on the old behaviour and validating the new version against evals before promoting it. Dated versions are not automatically safe to adopt blind, and breaking changes affect anyone consuming that version, not just floating aliases.

questions.question: You invoke Claude through a third-party vendor's hosted endpoint rather than the first-party API. Which statement is accurate?
options: The Messages API request and response shape stays consistent, but authentication, available headers, and some access patterns can differ by vendor
Third-party vendors run a completely different model that merely shares the same name
Streaming is only available through the first-party API
Tool use is unavailable when invoked through a third-party vendor
questions.explanation: Vendor-hosted access generally preserves the Messages API shape while differing in auth and some platform-specific details. It is the same model family, and streaming and tool use are not first-party exclusives.

questions.question: A single large system prompt is followed by a per-user profile block that changes daily, then the user's question. You want to cache as much as possible without caching stale profile data. What's the right move?
options: Place a cache breakpoint after the stable system prompt and a separate one after the profile block, so each stable segment is cached independently
Cache the whole assembled prompt as one block, accepting that the profile section forces a full cache miss every time it changes
Disable caching entirely since any dynamic content anywhere in the prompt invalidates the whole mechanism
Move the profile block after the user's question so it no longer matters where it sits
questions.explanation: Multiple cache breakpoints let you cache each stable segment independently, so the daily profile change only invalidates its own segment, not the whole prefix. Caching as one block or disabling it entirely wastes the win available from the stable system prompt, and moving the profile block after the question does not by itself fix cache segmentation.

questions.question: A 2,000-line 'do everything' prompt-handling function has become unreadable and every change risks breaking something else. What is the appropriate response?
options: Refactor incrementally into smaller, well-named functions with clear responsibilities, backed by tests, rather than rewriting from scratch
Leave it alone since prompt-handling code is inherently unstructurable
Rewrite it entirely from a blank file in one sitting with no tests
Add a large explanatory comment at the top and continue extending the function as before
questions.explanation: Incremental, tested refactoring reduces risk while improving structure, which is the standard response to a growing single-responsibility violation. A full rewrite with no tests risks losing behaviour, a comment does not fix the structural problem, and 'it can't be structured' is simply false.

questions.question: Two engineers each add a Claude-calling feature to the same file over the same sprint with no code review step. What SDLC practice is missing?
options: Code review integrated into the merge process, catching conflicting assumptions before they reach production
A larger context window, which would have let one engineer see the other's changes automatically
A more capable model, which would have resolved the conflicting assumptions on its own
Prompt caching, which prevents merge conflicts
questions.explanation: Code review is the SDLC step that catches conflicting assumptions before merge; skipping it is exactly what let two independent changes collide. Context window size, model capability, and caching do not address a missing human review step.

questions.question: A colleague claims 'zero-shot' means the model has zero context about the task. What's the accurate description?
options: Zero-shot means no worked examples are given, though task instructions can still be detailed; the model has no example demonstrations to pattern-match against
Zero-shot means the system prompt must be empty
Zero-shot means the model ignores the user's question entirely
Zero-shot only applies to classification tasks, never open-ended generation
questions.explanation: Zero-shot refers to the absence of example demonstrations, not the absence of instructions; you can still give detailed task instructions with zero examples. It does not require an empty system prompt, does not ignore the question, and applies beyond classification.

questions.question: A dashboard needs to show tokens streaming in over a persistent connection, with the server able to push updates without the client re-requesting. Which underlying technology is being described?
options: A websocket, which keeps a persistent bidirectional connection open
A one-off synchronous REST call repeated on a polling interval
The Message Batches API
A CDN cache
questions.explanation: A websocket provides the persistent, bidirectional connection needed for server-pushed streaming updates. Polling re-requests repeatedly rather than staying open, Batches is asynchronous and non-live, and a CDN cache serves static content rather than a live stream.

questions.question: A legal-document summarizer must catch subtle contractual nuance, and an internal wiki search bot just needs to find the right page fast. How should tiers differ?
options: Use a higher-capability tier for the nuanced legal task and a faster, cheaper tier for the simpler retrieval-style task
Use the same tier for both, since consistency across features matters more than matching capability to task difficulty
Use the cheapest tier for both to control cost uniformly
Use the highest tier for both to avoid any risk of missing something
questions.explanation: Matching tier to task difficulty is the core selection tradeoff: nuance-heavy work justifies a higher tier, and simple retrieval does not need it. Uniform tier choice in either direction either overpays or underserves one of the two tasks.

questions.question: You're deciding between running an agent yourself on your own infrastructure versus using an Anthropic-hosted managed agent deployment. What's the core tradeoff?
options: Self-hosting gives you full control over infrastructure and data flow at the cost of operating it yourself; a managed deployment reduces operational burden at the cost of less infrastructure control
There is no meaningful difference; both options run identically with identical operational responsibilities
Self-hosting is always cheaper regardless of the team's operational capacity
Managed deployment is only available for non-agentic use cases
questions.explanation: The tradeoff is control and operational burden versus convenience: self-hosting means you own the infrastructure, managed hosting shifts that operational load elsewhere. The two are not equivalent, cost depends on context rather than being universally lower for self-hosting, and managed deployment is squarely an agentic-use option.

questions.question: Which TWO are recognised agent design patterns for handling multi-step tasks?
options: A tool-use loop where the agent repeatedly calls tools and incorporates results until done
Delegating a bounded subtask to a subagent that returns a compact result
Hard-coding every possible input as its own branch so no runtime decision is ever needed
Disabling all tools to force the model to reason purely from its own knowledge
questions.explanation: The tool-use loop and subagent delegation are established agent patterns for multi-step work. Branching every possible input by hand is the workflow approach taken to an unworkable extreme, and disabling tools removes the agentic capability rather than patterning it.

questions.question: An assistant confidently states a statistic that sounds authoritative but cannot be traced to any source you gave it. What practice would have caught this before it reached the user?
options: Skepticism toward confident output: validate specific claims against your source material rather than trusting fluent, confident phrasing
Nothing; if the phrasing is confident and fluent, the content is reliable
Raising the temperature, since more varied phrasing tends to self-correct factual errors
Switching to a smaller model, which hallucinates less than larger ones
questions.explanation: Confident, fluent phrasing is not evidence of accuracy, so specific claims need validation against real sources. Trusting fluency is exactly the failure mode, temperature does not fix factual grounding, and model size alone does not guarantee lower hallucination rates.

questions.question: Your API client currently does `json.loads(response)` with no try/except. What is the minimum defensive-parsing improvement?
options: Wrap the parse in error handling, validate the parsed structure against an expected schema, and define a fallback for malformed output
Nothing needs to change as long as the prompt asks for JSON
Increase max_tokens so the JSON is less likely to be malformed
Add more few-shot examples of JSON output only, with no code-level changes at all
questions.explanation: Defensive parsing means handling the error, validating structure, and defining a fallback in code, since a prompt request alone does not guarantee conformance. max_tokens does not guarantee valid syntax, and examples help but do not substitute for code-level defense.

questions.question: A request reaches your Claude-powered admin panel with a valid session cookie. Before letting it delete a user account, what must you additionally verify?
options: Authorization: that this specific authenticated identity is permitted to perform this specific action, not merely that they are logged in at all
Nothing further; a valid session cookie is sufficient proof the action should proceed
Only that the request is over HTTPS
Only that the model itself agrees the action seems reasonable
questions.explanation: Authentication proves who someone is; authorization separately checks whether that identity may perform this specific action. A valid session alone does not establish permission, HTTPS protects transport not permission, and the model's own judgement is not an access control.

questions.question: Your content policy is enforced only by a single line in the system prompt. What is the recommended improvement per secure-by-design principles?
options: Layer independent enforcement: policy guidance in the prompt plus output-side filtering plus scoped tool permissions, so no single control is a single point of failure
Make the system-prompt line longer and more emphatic, since a sufficiently detailed instruction is an adequate standalone control
Remove the system-prompt line since it adds no value on its own
Rely on the user to self-police what they ask for
questions.explanation: Secure-by-design calls for layered, independent controls rather than one probabilistic instruction. A longer prompt line is still a single, bypassable layer, removing it entirely drops even that layer, and user self-policing is not a control at all.

questions.question: You want a guarantee that a specific shell command can never run, no matter what the agent decides mid-session. Which mechanism actually provides a guarantee, as opposed to a strong suggestion?
options: A hook that deterministically intercepts and blocks the command before execution
A detailed system-prompt paragraph forbidding that command
Choosing a model known for being cautious
Setting a lower temperature for that session
questions.explanation: A hook enforces deterministically at the point of execution, which is what a guarantee requires. A prompt instruction, a cautious model, or a lower temperature are all probabilistic and can be overridden by circumstances the guidance did not anticipate.

questions.question: Your team wants to know, after the fact, exactly which service account accessed a sensitive internal tool and when. What capability does this require?
options: Authorized access monitoring and logging tied to identity, so actions can be attributed and reviewed after the fact
A larger context window, so the model remembers who called it
A single shared service account for simplicity
Prompt caching on the tool's description
questions.explanation: After-the-fact attribution requires identity-tied access logging and monitoring. Context window size has nothing to do with audit trails, a single shared account destroys attributability, and caching a description is unrelated to access logs.

questions.question: You are designing a tool set for an agent and want to minimise wrong-tool selection from the start, before any bugs appear in production. Which practice addresses this proactively?
options: Write each tool's description to be mutually distinct, including when not to use it, and keep the tool set focused rather than sprawling
Add as many tools as possible upfront so the agent has maximum flexibility for any future task
Give every tool an identical, generic description so the agent isn't biased toward any one of them
Rely on the model's general judgement and skip writing descriptions with much detail
questions.explanation: Distinct, well-scoped descriptions with explicit boundaries are the proactive defense against wrong-tool selection. A sprawling tool set or generic descriptions both increase ambiguity, and skipping detail leaves the model with nothing to disambiguate on.

questions.question: A tool call fails because the downstream service is temporarily down. What should the tool return to the agent?
options: A structured error indicating the failure is transient and retriable, distinct from a permanent or invalid-input failure
An empty string with no further information
The same generic error message regardless of whether the failure is temporary or permanent
A silently truncated partial result with no indication anything went wrong
questions.explanation: A structured, categorised error lets the agent decide to retry, wait, or escalate appropriately. An empty string or generic message gives no actionable signal, and a silent partial result actively misleads the agent into treating a failure as success.

questions.question: An MCP server exposes a large static company glossary that Claude should be able to read into context when relevant, without the model needing to invoke an action to fetch it each time. Which MCP primitive fits best?
options: A resource
A tool, since any content the model uses must be fetched through an explicit tool call
A prompt template
A transport setting
questions.explanation: Resources are the MCP primitive for exposing readable reference data the model can pull into context. Tools represent actions rather than passive reference data, prompts are user-invoked templates, and a transport is the communication channel, not content.

questions.question: A capability needs to call three different internal REST services with complex auth, be reused across five separate Claude applications, and be maintained by a dedicated platform team. Which approach fits best?
options: An MCP server, maintained centrally and connected to by each of the five applications
A Skill duplicated into each of the five applications' repositories
Five separate hand-written custom tools, one per application, kept manually in sync
One shared, hardcoded block of instructions pasted into each application's system prompt
questions.explanation: Centralized maintenance, complex auth, and reuse across many applications is exactly the MCP server case. Duplicating a Skill or hand-syncing five custom tools both create maintenance burden the centralized server avoids, and pasted instructions cannot perform authenticated REST calls at all.

questions.question: A task's steps are mostly fixed, but one step occasionally needs the agent to choose between two valid approaches based on data it hasn't seen before. How should this be architected?
options: A workflow overall, with a small bounded agentic decision point only at the one variable step
A fully autonomous agent for every step, since any variability anywhere means the whole task should be agentic
A rigid workflow with no agentic step, requiring a human to manually pick the approach every time
Two entirely separate hard-coded workflows, one per possible approach, chosen at random
questions.explanation: Mostly-fixed steps with one point of genuine judgement call for a workflow with a small bounded agentic decision, not a wholesale switch to autonomy. Full autonomy overcorrects for one variable point, a fully rigid workflow can't make the judgement call at all, and random selection ignores the data meant to inform the choice.

questions.question: A capability is purely a set of written instructions and reference examples for how to format a specific report, used only within Claude Code by one team, with no external system to call. Which approach fits, and why not an MCP server?
options: A Skill; there is no external capability or live system to expose, so a server would add operational overhead for no benefit
An MCP server, because any reusable capability should default to a server regardless of whether it calls anything external
A custom tool, since tools are the default choice whenever multiple people will use something
Hard-coded into CLAUDE.md with no other structure, since it's team-specific
questions.explanation: Instructions and reference material with nothing external to call is the textbook Skill case; standing up a server here adds cost with no corresponding capability gained. Tools represent actions rather than formatting guidance, and while CLAUDE.md could hold some of this, a Skill is the structured, reusable form built for exactly this need.

questions.question: Which TWO of these are examples of output constraints, as distinct from few-shot examples?
options: Specifying a maximum word count and a required set of JSON fields
Requiring the response to omit any preamble and start directly with the answer
Showing three worked input-output pairs before the real task
Explaining the company's mission statement for context
questions.explanation: A word limit and required field set, plus a no-preamble rule, are direct constraints on the shape of the output. Worked pairs are few-shot examples rather than constraints, and a mission-statement explanation is background context, not a constraint on output form.

questions.question: A prompt buries the single most important instruction in the middle of six paragraphs of background. The model keeps missing it. What is the most direct fix?
options: Move the critical instruction to the beginning or end of the prompt, where models attend most reliably, and trim unnecessary background
Repeat the six paragraphs of background twice so the instruction gets more total exposure
Switch to a lower temperature so the model reads more carefully
Add the instruction as a sixth occurrence in the middle so it appears more often
questions.explanation: Long inputs are read less reliably in the middle, so critical instructions belong at the start or end, with unneeded background trimmed. Doubling background or repeating mid-document placement does not fix the position problem, and temperature does not affect positional attention.

questions.question: Two independent subagents each need a large shared reference document to complete their separate parts of a task, but the documents should not pollute each other's follow-up reasoning with the other's intermediate steps.
options: Give each subagent its own isolated context containing the shared reference, so their intermediate reasoning never crosses over
Run both subagents in a single shared context so they can see each other's reasoning as it happens
Give the reference document to only one subagent and have it verbally summarise the whole thing to the other
Skip giving the document to either and let both reason from general knowledge instead
questions.explanation: Context isolation through separate subagent contexts lets each hold the shared reference without their intermediate reasoning bleeding together. A single shared context defeats the isolation goal, one subagent narrating to the other loses fidelity, and skipping the reference entirely abandons the actual source material.

questions.question: A moderation feature must flag live chat messages in under a second, and separately re-score the entire message archive once a month for a compliance report. How should these two needs be split?
options: Synchronous calls for live moderation; the Batches API for the monthly archive re-score
Batches API for both, since consolidating everything onto one API path simplifies the codebase
Synchronous calls for both, accepting the higher cost on the monthly re-score to avoid maintaining two code paths
Streaming for the monthly re-score, since streaming is the cheapest option regardless of urgency
questions.explanation: Each workload matches its own SLA: live moderation needs realtime response, and the tolerant monthly job belongs on Batches for cost. Consolidating either way sacrifices either latency or cost for no real benefit, and streaming does not reduce per-token cost.

questions.question: Which TWO scenarios genuinely justify the Batches API over synchronous calls?
options: Re-indexing a document library overnight with no user waiting on the result
Scoring a backlog of 200,000 support tickets for a weekly dashboard
Answering a customer's question in a live chat widget
Validating a form field as the user types
questions.explanation: Both are large, latency-tolerant jobs with no one waiting on an immediate response, the batch sweet spot. Live chat and as-you-type validation both need an immediate synchronous response.

questions.question: A new model version is released with materially better reasoning but a documented change to how it escapes special characters in code output. Your pipeline parses that output with regex tuned to the old escaping. What is the safe migration path?
options: Test the new version against your parser and eval suite in staging, update the regex if needed, then promote deliberately
Upgrade in production immediately, since better reasoning always outweighs a small formatting difference
Ignore the new version permanently to avoid ever touching the parser again
Turn off the parser and pass raw output straight to users
questions.explanation: A documented breaking change to output formatting demands validating and adjusting the dependent code before promotion. Upgrading blind risks silently breaking the parser, permanently freezing loses real capability gains, and disabling the parser abandons validation entirely.

questions.question: You want to forecast next quarter's Claude spend for a feature that's growing 15% month over month. What inputs does a sound cost model need?
options: Historical token usage per request, the growth rate, and current per-token pricing, projected forward
Only the current month's total invoice, extrapolated by guesswork
The number of engineers on the team
The size of the context window, regardless of how much of it is actually used per call
questions.explanation: A cost model needs actual usage data, a growth assumption, and pricing, projected forward systematically. Team size is irrelevant to spend, a single invoice extrapolated by guesswork lacks a growth basis, and window size alone says nothing about tokens actually consumed.

questions.question: An agent has both a client-side tool (reads the user's current form input) and a server-side tool (queries a production database). A refactor accidentally swaps their execution locations. What breaks first?
options: The tool meant to read live client state can no longer see it once it's forced to run server-side, since the server has no visibility into the user's in-browser state
Nothing breaks, since tools are interchangeable regardless of where they execute
Only latency changes; both tools still function identically otherwise
The database tool becomes faster once running client-side
questions.explanation: Client-side tools depend on access to the user's local browser state, which a server cannot see; swapping execution location breaks that access entirely. Tools are not interchangeable across execution boundaries, and a database query running client-side would typically fail or be insecure, not simply run faster.

questions.question: A single tool named handle_request currently does lookup, validation, and notification all in one call, and the agent frequently gets confused about what result it will get back. What is the most direct fix?
options: Split it into three focused tools, each with one clear responsibility and a description that reflects it
Rename the tool to something more exciting so it's memorable to the model
Add a fourth responsibility so it's clearly the 'do everything' tool
Leave the tool as is but add a longer usage example in the system prompt
questions.explanation: Splitting an overloaded tool into focused, single-responsibility tools with matching descriptions removes the ambiguity about what each call returns. Renaming or adding more responsibilities does not address the confusion, and a longer example patches around a design problem rather than fixing it.

questions.question: A workflow currently branches on eleven different document types with a dedicated code path for each, and a twelfth type just appeared with no existing path. The team's instinct is to add a twelfth branch. What should you consider instead?
options: Whether the branching factor itself signals this is now agent territory, since new document types keep appearing faster than branches can be written
Immediately writing the twelfth branch, since workflows should always be extended to cover every new case as it appears
Deleting all eleven existing branches and starting over with no clear replacement
Ignoring the twelfth document type entirely until a branch is convenient to write
questions.explanation: A workflow whose branch count keeps growing faster than you can maintain is the signal to reconsider the architecture, not just add branch twelve. Endless branch-adding is the losing race that motivated the reconsideration, deleting everything with no plan is reckless, and ignoring new input types loses real work.

questions.question: You're deciding whether to build a custom agent loop from scratch or use the Claude Agent SDK. Your team has no existing orchestration code and a tight deadline. What does the SDK offer that changes the calculus?
options: Built-in handling for the tool-use loop, context management, and common agent patterns, reducing what you must build and test yourself
A completely different model with different capabilities than the raw API
Guaranteed lower per-token pricing versus calling the API directly
Automatic conversion of any workflow into an agent regardless of whether that fits the task
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK provides scaffolding for the loop and common patterns, cutting the amount of custom orchestration code a tight deadline would otherwise require. It is the same underlying model family, does not change per-token pricing, and does not override the workflow-versus-agent decision for you.

questions.question: A tone-of-voice instruction sits in the system prompt, and a conflicting tone instruction appears in the user's message. Which generally takes precedence, and why does this matter for design?
options: The system prompt is the higher-priority, more durable placement, so critical constraints belong there rather than relying on user messages to enforce them
The user message always overrides the system prompt with no exceptions in any case
Whichever instruction is longer wins
Neither takes precedence; the model picks arbitrarily and this is unpredictable by design
questions.explanation: The system prompt carries durable priority, which is exactly why critical constraints belong there rather than being left to a user message to reinforce. Length is not the deciding factor, and precedence is not arbitrary, it follows deliberate placement.

questions.question: Your instructions ask the model to 'be concise,' but responses stay long regardless. What refinement is more likely to work?
options: Replace the vague adjective with a specific constraint, such as a maximum sentence or word count
Repeat the word 'concise' several times in the same sentence for emphasis
Remove the instruction entirely, since vague adjectives never influence length at all
Switch to a different model tier without changing the instruction
questions.explanation: A concrete constraint gives the model something specific to satisfy, unlike a vague adjective open to interpretation. Repetition of the same vague word does not add precision, dropping the instruction abandons the goal, and a tier swap does not fix an underspecified constraint.

questions.question: An agent's context contains the full text of 12 API responses from earlier tool calls, most of which are no longer relevant to the current step, and quality is degrading. What is the appropriate context management move?
options: Prune the stale tool outputs, keeping only what remains relevant to the current step, to reclaim budget and reduce noise
Leave all 12 in place since removing any tool output risks losing information the agent might need eventually
Add a 13th tool call to compensate
Switch to a smaller model so the existing context fits more comfortably
questions.explanation: Pruning stale, no-longer-relevant tool outputs is the direct fix for both budget pressure and quality degradation from noise. Keeping everything indefinitely is what caused the problem, adding another call adds more clutter, and a smaller model does not resolve an oversized, noisy context.

questions.question: Your application's schema for a structured extraction task has 40 optional fields, and the model frequently fills in plausible-looking but incorrect values for fields that weren't actually present in the source document. What design issue does this point to?
options: The schema likely needs a way to represent 'field not found' explicitly, rather than forcing a value into every field regardless of whether it's supported by the input
The model tier is too small and should simply be upgraded
The document input format is unsupported
The schema has too few fields and should be expanded further
questions.explanation: Forcing a value into every field encourages fabrication when the source lacks that data; an explicit null or not-found representation lets the model report absence honestly. Model tier is not the driver of a schema design gap, the input format is not implicated, and adding more fields compounds rather than fixes the issue.

questions.question: Multiple features in your app each maintain their own separate conversation with Claude for the same end user, and none of them share any awareness of the others. A user complains the assistant 'forgets' things between features. What's the actual architecture answer here?
options: This may be an intentional design tradeoff: some features genuinely warrant separate, isolated conversations, and cross-feature memory is a distinct feature to design deliberately if wanted, not an automatic default
Every feature must always share one giant conversation so nothing is ever forgotten
The context window is too small and must be increased before anything else can be considered
This is always a bug that must be fixed by merging all conversations
questions.explanation: Session boundaries are a design choice: isolated conversations per feature are often correct for scoping and privacy, and shared cross-feature memory, if wanted, needs to be built deliberately rather than assumed. Forcing one shared conversation ignores legitimate isolation needs, window size is not the driver here, and calling it an automatic bug skips the actual design tradeoff.

questions.question: A document-processing agent reads uploaded files from anonymous users before any human review. Which TWO practices reduce the risk of those files carrying manipulative embedded instructions?
options: Treat uploaded file content as untrusted data, isolated from the agent's own instructions
Scope the agent's available actions tightly, so even a manipulated read cannot trigger a sensitive operation
Trust the content fully once the file passes a virus scan, since malware and prompt injection are the same category of risk
Increase the model's context window so it can read the whole file at once
questions.explanation: Isolating untrusted file content from trusted instructions, plus tightly scoping available actions, are the two levers that blunt embedded manipulation. A virus scan addresses malware, not textual injection, which is a different risk entirely, and context window size has no bearing on injection resistance.

questions.question: A user directly asks your assistant, in plain conversation, to roleplay as an unrestricted version of itself with no rules. Is this the same category of risk as a webpage with hidden malicious instructions, and does it need the same fix?
options: No; this is a jailbreak attempt via direct conversation, addressed through policy and refusal training, whereas the webpage case is injection via untrusted content, addressed through isolation and least privilege
Yes; both are identical attacks solved by the exact same single technical control
No; the direct request is not a risk at all since the user is a legitimate, authenticated party
Yes, but only because both involve text
questions.explanation: These are genuinely distinct risk categories with distinct mitigations: jailbreak attempts are handled through the model's own policy and refusal behaviour, while content injection is handled through isolating untrusted data and limiting what it can trigger. Being authenticated does not make a jailbreak attempt harmless, and 'both involve text' is too shallow a similarity to imply one fix covers both.

questions.question: Your team is deciding where to place a content-policy check: only once, at the very end after the full response is generated, or additionally earlier in the pipeline. What does layering suggest?
options: Check at multiple points, since an end-only check misses the chance to prevent an issue earlier and provides no depth if that single check is bypassed or misses something
A single end-of-pipeline check is always sufficient and additional checks are pure redundancy with no value
Policy checks should only ever run on user input, never on the model's own output
Policy checks are unnecessary if the system prompt already states the policy
questions.explanation: Layered guardrails at multiple points reduce reliance on any single check catching everything. A lone end check has no backup if it fails, restricting checks to input-only ignores output-side risk entirely, and a system-prompt statement alone is a probabilistic control, not a full guardrail.

questions.question: A contractor's temporary access to your Claude API key needs to end automatically when their contract does, without anyone remembering to manually revoke it. What capability addresses this?
options: Scoped, time-limited credentials or access grants tied to identity, rather than a long-lived shared key with indefinite validity
A stronger password on the shared key
Asking the contractor to delete the key from their notes when they leave
Increasing the rate limit on the key so contractor usage doesn't interfere with production traffic
questions.explanation: Time-bound, identity-scoped credentials expire on their own, removing the dependence on someone remembering to revoke access manually. A stronger password does not add an expiry, relying on the departing contractor to self-revoke is not a control, and rate limits address throughput, not access lifecycle.

questions.question: A multi-step agent produces a wrong final report. The trace shows the retrieval tool returned the correct documents, and the model's summary of them is accurate, but a formatting tool downstream truncated the summary mid-sentence before it reached the user. Where is the fault?
options: In the formatting tool or its integration into the pipeline, since both retrieval and model reasoning were correct up to that point
In the model's reasoning, since a wrong final report always originates from the model regardless of what the trace shows
In the retrieval tool, since it's the earliest step and therefore always the first thing to suspect
In the user's original request, since it must have been ambiguous
questions.explanation: Tracing shows the fault entering exactly where the truncation occurred, downstream of correct retrieval and correct model reasoning, so the formatting tool or its wiring is where to look. Blaming the model or the earliest step by default ignores what the trace actually shows, and nothing in the trace implicates the original request.

questions.question: An error handler currently catches every exception type identically and always tells the user to 'try again later,' whether the cause is a bad user input, a rate limit, or a permanent server error. What is the improvement?
options: Classify errors by type and recoverability, and choose the recovery strategy and user-facing message per category rather than one generic response
Keep the single generic message, since users don't need to know the distinction between error types
Log the errors in more detail internally without changing what the user is ever told
Remove error handling entirely and let exceptions surface raw to the user
questions.explanation: Different error categories call for different recovery strategies and different user messaging, which a single blanket response cannot provide. Users benefit from knowing whether to retry, fix input, or wait, better internal logging alone doesn't change the poor user experience, and removing handling entirely is a regression, not an improvement.

questions.question: You're choosing a transport for an MCP server that will be called by a client on a different machine over the network, with no requirement for a persistent open connection between calls. Which fits best, and why not stdio?
options: An HTTP-based transport, since it supports request-based network communication; stdio assumes a local subprocess sharing standard input and output on the same machine
stdio, since it works over any network as long as both machines are on the same subnet
Either works identically regardless of whether the client and server share a machine
A raw TCP socket is the only valid choice for any MCP server
questions.explanation: HTTP-based transport fits a remote, request-oriented client-server relationship; stdio is designed for a local subprocess communicating over shared standard input and output, not cross-machine networking. The two transports are not interchangeable regardless of topology, and MCP is not limited to raw TCP sockets as the only network option.

questions.question: Your MCP server currently returns raw, unvalidated data straight from an upstream API to Claude, including occasional malformed records. What server-side practice would improve robustness?
options: Validate and normalise the data before returning it, so malformed upstream records don't reach the model as if they were clean
Pass everything through unchanged, since validation is solely the responsibility of whichever application calls the server
Stop returning any data at all if the upstream service is ever imperfect
Cache the malformed records so they are returned consistently every time
questions.explanation: A well-built server validates and normalises what it returns, rather than passing upstream imperfections straight through as if clean. Deferring entirely to the calling application ignores the server's own responsibility, refusing all data over occasional flaws is an overcorrection, and caching malformed records preserves the very problem being raised.

questions.question: A capability must call a live, authenticated internal API and also needs to be reachable identically from three unrelated internal tools your company builds. Weighing Skills, custom tools, and MCP, which fits, and what rules out a Skill here?
options: An MCP server; a Skill is instructional content and cannot itself make authenticated live API calls on its own
A Skill, since Skills can natively perform any authenticated API call given the right description
A custom tool duplicated by hand into each of the three consuming tools
None of the three approaches fit a live authenticated API
questions.explanation: Live, authenticated API access reused across multiple consumers is the MCP server case; a Skill is packaged instructions and reference material, not a mechanism for making live authenticated calls itself. Hand-duplicating a custom tool three times creates the exact maintenance burden a shared server avoids, and this is squarely within scope for one of the three approaches.

questions.question: A team wants to add Claude-based text classification to an existing synchronous request-handling pipeline that currently blocks on every I/O call. What foundational concern should be addressed before adding the new blocking API call?
options: Whether the pipeline should move to asynchronous, non-blocking I/O so a slow classification call doesn't stall unrelated requests
Whether the classification labels should be stored as strings or integers
Whether the git branch naming convention should change
Whether the team's code editor supports syntax highlighting for the new code
questions.explanation: Adding another blocking network call to an already-blocking pipeline is exactly the concurrency concern to address before shipping, since one slow call would otherwise stall unrelated work. Label storage format, branch naming, and editor tooling are unrelated to the concurrency risk being introduced.

questions.question: Which of these activities most clearly belongs to the design phase rather than the build or operate phases of the systems life cycle?
options: Deciding the overall architecture, including workflow-versus-agent tradeoffs and model tier selection, before writing implementation code
Fixing a production incident that occurred last night
Writing the actual integration code against the chosen API
Monitoring live cost dashboards after launch
questions.explanation: Architectural decisions made before implementation begins are squarely design-phase work. Fixing an incident and monitoring dashboards are operate-phase activities, and writing the integration code is build-phase, both of which come after design decisions are made.

questions.question: A requirement states 'the system must respond quickly.' What is missing that would make this usable for design and testing?
options: A concrete, measurable target, such as a specific latency percentile under a specific load, so it can be checked objectively
Nothing; 'quickly' is specific enough to design and test against directly
A list of every possible future feature the system might ever need
The name of the engineer responsible for writing the code
questions.explanation: A vague adjective like 'quickly' cannot be checked without a concrete, measurable target such as a latency percentile under a defined load. It is not sufficiently specific as written, an exhaustive future feature list is unrelated to this gap, and naming an engineer does not make the requirement testable.

questions.question: An agent's memory currently holds every tool call and result from the entire session with no pruning, and by turn 40 the agent starts repeating earlier mistakes it should have already learned from. What does this suggest about how memory is being used?
options: Raw accumulation without summarisation or structuring may bury the useful signal in volume, so what's kept needs curating, not just retained indefinitely
Memory should be disabled entirely, since any memory clearly makes agents worse over time
The agent needs a larger context window and nothing else needs to change
The problem is unrelated to memory and is purely a model-capability issue
questions.explanation: Unstructured accumulation can bury useful signal under volume; the fix is curating what's retained rather than keeping everything indefinitely or dropping memory altogether. A bigger window without curation still drowns in the same noise, and this is a memory-management issue, not simply a capability ceiling.

questions.question: A publishing pipeline always validates rights, formats a manuscript, and records approval. Its middle stage lets Claude investigate unusual citation problems with tools until it has enough evidence. How should this architecture be characterized?
options: It must be classified only as an agent because one stage chooses tool steps dynamically at runtime.
It is a workflow containing a bounded agentic stage for the open-ended investigation.
It is merely one augmented model call because every stage ultimately serves one manuscript.
It is parallelization because the deterministic stages and investigation belong to the same pipeline.
questions.explanation: Workflow and agent patterns compose: deterministic stages can bound an agent where adaptive exploration is valuable.

questions.question: A procurement system always verifies required fields and approval limits, but it lets Claude investigate unusual supplier notes using whichever read-only sources seem relevant. What best describes the overall design?
options: A pure agent because any model-directed step makes the whole control structure agentic
A pure workflow because fixed approval checks make all steps predetermined
A retrieval system because supplier information sources are read before approval
A hybrid design with deterministic controls around an agentic investigation step
questions.explanation: Hybrid designs keep predictable business rules fixed while granting autonomy only where the path genuinely varies.

questions.question: A research parent agent delegates document analysis to a specialist. The specialist returns its full reasoning transcript plus hundreds of raw excerpts, repeatedly crowding out the parent's task context. What boundary change is best?
options: Increase every specialist's output limit so no excerpts are truncated
Copy the parent's complete transcript into the specialist before every delegation
Require a structured findings handoff with citations and only task-relevant excerpts
Train a separate model on all prior specialist transcripts each week
questions.explanation: A bounded handoff transfers decision-relevant evidence while keeping the specialist's internal transcript outside the parent context.

questions.question: Two inventory sub-agents can independently reserve the same last unit while a coordinator waits for both. The team wants parallel analysis without duplicate reservations. Which design addresses the agent-pattern failure?
options: Give both sub-agents the reservation tool and ask them explicitly in their prompts to avoid choosing the same unit.
Let each sub-agent reserve optimistically and have the coordinator keep whichever response contains more confident language.
Copy the inventory snapshot into both contexts and require each sub-agent to return its updated copy afterward.
Let sub-agents propose candidates, but centralize reservation through one authoritative service with atomic conflict handling.
questions.explanation: Parallel agents can perform read-only analysis, while a single authoritative mutation boundary prevents conflicting reservations.

questions.question: An infrastructure agent alternates between inspecting a service and proposing the same ineffective repair. Each tool call succeeds, so the loop never reaches a terminal answer. What should the harness do?
options: Enforce iteration or cost limits, detect nonprogress, and escalate with an incomplete-status record.
Allow unlimited turns because successful tool execution proves the agent is making useful progress.
Stop after an arbitrary turn and mark the repair complete without checking service state.
Increase the context window so repeated actions eventually become a valid repair plan.
questions.explanation: Deterministic budgets and nonprogress handling bound autonomous execution without falsely reporting task success.

questions.question: A coding parent agent delegates a database migration draft to a specialist. The specialist reports success, but its generated file exists only in an isolated workspace the parent cannot access. What design change addresses the failure?
options: Trust the specialist's success message and recreate the file from memory
Define an explicit artifact handoff or deliberately shared workspace boundary
Give the specialist more reasoning tokens before it writes the migration
Store the parent's conversation history in long-term semantic memory
questions.explanation: Sub-agent isolation requires an intentional mechanism for returning files or placing them in an authorized shared location.

questions.question: A news-research agent may choose sources and follow leads, but editorial policy allows at most ten source fetches per assignment. Where should that fixed limit live?
options: Only in the system prompt so Claude can interpret exceptions flexibly
Inside the source-selection sub-agent's private reasoning and nowhere else
In the harness or workflow state that counts and blocks excess fetches
In a larger context window reserved for all fetched source text
questions.explanation: The agent can choose which sources matter while deterministic orchestration enforces the non-negotiable fetch ceiling.

questions.question: A multi-tenant travel agent retrieves durable memories by semantic similarity. A preference saved for one company appears in another company's planning session because both use the same memory collection. What is the essential correction?
options: Ask the model to ignore memories mentioning a different company name
Namespace memory storage and retrieval by authenticated tenant and user scope
Raise the similarity threshold until fewer saved preferences are returned
Summarize each company's preferences into a shorter shared memory record
questions.explanation: Enforcing tenant and user scope at the memory boundary prevents cross-tenant candidates from being retrieved at all.

questions.question: A platform team allows Claude Code to run read-only Terraform commands but must block every terraform apply, including attempts triggered by repository content. Which control best enforces the boundary?
options: Add a bold warning to CLAUDE.md stating that apply commands are forbidden in all circumstances.
Select the most capable model because stronger reasoning makes command prohibitions mechanically enforceable.
Ask Claude to print each Terraform command twice so a human can notice dangerous operations.
Configure a PreToolUse hook that rejects Bash calls matching the prohibited apply command.
questions.explanation: A blocking pre-tool hook evaluates the attempted action at execution time and can deterministically deny matching commands.

questions.question: A benefits platform requires that no applicant be approved unless a deterministic eligibility service confirms every statutory condition. How should Claude participate in the approval flow?
options: Let Claude approve directly after placing the statutory conditions in a high-priority system instruction.
Let Claude approve directly whenever its explanation mentions each statutory condition by name.
Let Claude approve directly when the model assigns its own confidence above a configured threshold.
Use Claude to extract and explain the case, but let the eligibility service authorize approval.
questions.explanation: This design uses Claude for language-heavy work while preserving the explicit requirement that deterministic code owns authorization.

questions.question: A team's root CLAUDE.md has grown to 1,800 lines covering every framework convention, every past architectural decision, and every edge case ever encountered. What configuration-management problem does this create, and what is the fix?
options: The file size only matters for git repository size, not for how Claude actually processes it during a session.
There is no downside beyond aesthetics; larger CLAUDE.md files simply give Claude more information to work with, which can only help.
The fix is to delete CLAUDE.md entirely and rely only on in-conversation instructions each session.

Because CLAUDE.md content is concatenated into context on every session, a bloated file burns tokens and dilutes model attention on every turn; the fix is decomposing detail into @import-ed or path-scoped rule files, keeping the root file as a lean, high-level index.
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is loaded and paid for in tokens on every session; the documented fix for bloat is modular decomposition via imports and path-scoped rules, not a single ever-growing file.

questions.question: A fintech service calls Claude, then executes a create_refund tool against a payment provider. A network timeout occurs after the provider may have accepted the refund. What design prevents an application retry from issuing a second refund?
options: Ask Claude to remember whether it created the refund and trust its next response as the transaction record.
Disable all retries so a timeout can never cause the application to send another payment-provider request.
Increase max_tokens so Claude can include enough explanation for the payment provider to deduplicate each request.
Generate a stable operation key, persist it, and reuse it with the provider's idempotency or status-check mechanism.
questions.explanation: A persisted operation identity lets retries resolve an ambiguous outcome without creating the same external side effect twice.

questions.question: A hospital requirement says analytics may receive diagnosis categories but never raw clinician notes. The team is translating that requirement into the Claude application's implementation. What design makes the rule verifiable?
options: Define a typed category-only output contract, enforce redaction before analytics, and test the boundary with representative inputs.
Tell Claude in the prompt never to mention any notes, then send its unrestricted response directly into analytics.
Choose Opus for the classification because higher capability eliminates the need for downstream field restrictions.
Store the full notes in analytics but document that dashboards should display only diagnosis categories.
questions.explanation: The requirement becomes verifiable when the data contract, enforcement point, and acceptance checks all encode the prohibited flow.

questions.question: An expense service base64-encodes receipt photos that are actually JPEG files but sets each image block's media_type to image/png in the request. Extraction results come back garbled or the request errors. What is the correct fix?
options: Re-save every receipt as an actual PNG before sending, since the media_type is right and the underlying files simply need to be converted to match the declared image/png format that the request already specifies.
Lower the resolution of the receipt images before encoding, on the theory that oversized image data is what corrupts the decode step and produces the garbled extraction output.
Set each image block's media_type to image/jpeg so the declared type matches the actual bytes, because the API decodes the base64 data according to that declaration and a mismatch corrupts the image.
Add more few-shot examples of correctly extracted receipts to the prompt, so the model learns the target fields well enough to recover the values despite the malformed image input.
questions.explanation: The declared media_type must match the true encoding of the bytes; correcting it to image/jpeg lets the data decode properly, resolving the garbled or failed extraction.

questions.question: A document team sends a single full-page 8000x6000 scan and asks Claude to read tiny footer print. The image is within the file-size limit, yet Claude consistently misses or misreads the footer. What limitation explains this and what is the fix?
options: The file exceeded a hard pixel-count ceiling and was rejected before analysis, so the model saw nothing at all; the fix is to compress the scan until it slips under the maximum allowed dimensions.
Extended thinking was not enabled, so the model lacked the reasoning budget to decode small text; turning on thinking gives it enough steps to resolve the footer characters accurately.

The scan should be sent at maximum JPEG quality with no compression, since compression artifacts are what blur the footer text and a lossless encode will preserve the small characters for the model to read.

Large images are downscaled before the model sees them, so fine print is lost even under the size limit; crop the footer region and send it as a separate higher-effective-resolution image (tile the page) to preserve the small text.
questions.explanation: The governing limit is effective resolution after downscaling, not file size; tiling the region of interest so the small text occupies more of the model's usable pixels is the fix.

questions.question: A contract-extraction batch of 5,000 requests ends. The importer treats any request whose result type is not errored as a clean success and writes its output straight to the database. Some fields later turn out truncated mid-JSON. What did the importer overlook?
options: Batch results are returned in submission order, so the importer should have matched each output to its input by array index rather than trusting the succeeded flag it read.
The batch as a whole reports a single status, so a partial-failure batch should have been discarded entirely and resubmitted rather than importing any of its individual results.

A request that hits the token ceiling is still a succeeded result with stop_reason of max_tokens, so the importer must inspect each result's stop_reason and reject truncated outputs, not just filter out errored entries.
Truncation means the batch expired before finishing, so the importer should have raised the batch's overall timeout ceiling and resubmitted the affected job for a longer processing window.
questions.explanation: The governing point is that 'not errored' is not 'complete': a succeeded batch result can carry stop_reason max_tokens and thus truncated JSON, which per-result validation must catch.

questions.domain: Claude Md Does Not Set Api Model
questions.question: A team writes Always use claude-sonnet-5 for all work in their project CLAUDE.md, expecting it to pin the model everywhere. Their Claude Code sessions comply, but their backend Messages API service keeps sending whatever model string the code passes. Why, and what is the right fix?
options: CLAUDE.md guidance shapes Claude Code behavior but never selects the model for API requests; the backend's model is a request parameter, so pin it in the service's code or configuration, not in prose.
The CLAUDE.md instruction is being overridden by a higher-precedence enterprise memory file, so the fix is to move the pin into an enterprise-level CLAUDE.md that outranks the project one.

The backend needs the instruction inside its system prompt on every call, since placing the same sentence in the system prompt makes Claude choose and hold to claude-sonnet-5 for that request and every subsequent turn in the exchange.
CLAUDE.md only loads for files inside the repository, so the fix is to add the backend's runtime directory to the memory search path so the pin is discovered at request time.
questions.explanation: The model on a Messages API call is set by the model field in the request, independent of any CLAUDE.md. Configuration must live where it is actually read -- the API request.

questions.question: A team stores a third-party service's API token inside the project's committed CLAUDE.md so Claude Code 'has it handy' every session. Why is that the wrong configuration home for the value?
options: CLAUDE.md is committed context fed to the model, not a secret store, so the token reaches anyone with repo access
CLAUDE.md is loaded only for the first session of the day, so the token would be unavailable on later runs anyway
CLAUDE.md entries are truncated after a fixed character length, so a long token value would be silently cut off mid-string
CLAUDE.md is ignored unless the same token is also duplicated into the user-level directory for precedence to resolve
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is versioned project context that anyone cloning the repo can read; secrets belong in environment variables or a secret manager, never committed context.

questions.question: A retail app sends a shelf photo and asks Claude for the exact count of every product facing, expecting inventory-grade precision. Counts drift on densely stocked shelves. What should the team conclude?
options: The image must be re-sent as several cropped tiles, after which the model's per-tile counts become exactly correct
Turning on a dedicated object-detection parameter switches the vision path into a precise, count-guaranteed mode
Vision reasoning is approximate for dense fine-grained counting and is not a substitute for a dedicated counting system
The drift is caused by JPEG compression alone, so re-sending the same shelf as a lossless PNG will yield exact counts
questions.explanation: The model estimates rather than tallies; for exact inventory counts the sound design pairs vision with a deterministic detection/counting pipeline.

questions.question: An administrator's managed Claude Code settings deny Bash(curl *). A project later adds an allow rule for the same command pattern. What should happen when Claude attempts the command?
options: The project allow rule wins because project settings are closer to the working directory.
Claude chooses between the rules based on which instruction appears later in its context.
The two rules cancel out, so Claude runs the command once and asks only on later attempts.
The command remains blocked because managed policy and matching deny rules cannot be relaxed by the project.
questions.explanation: Managed configuration establishes the organizational boundary, and a matching deny rule takes precedence over lower-level allows.

questions.question: A Claude Code plugin ships a JavaScript hook that imports third-party packages. The author committed package.json beside the hook and assumes plugin installation will run npm install, but the hook fails on a clean machine. What should the plugin do?
options: Move package.json into .claude-plugin/ because manifest discovery automatically installs all packages found inside that directory.
Import the required packages through CLAUDE.md so Claude Code downloads them while loading the project instructions.
Use a setup hook to check dependencies on first use and install missing packages under CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA.
Require developers to install the packages globally because plugin hooks resolve only global Node modules.
questions.explanation: A setup hook can perform explicit first-use dependency installation, while the plugin data directory provides persistent plugin-scoped storage.

questions.question: A direct SSE parser throws an exception whenever it sees an event type outside its fixed allowlist. After the API adds a nonterminal metadata event, otherwise valid streams fail. How should the parser be hardened?
options: Treat every unfamiliar event as message_stop so all current content is preserved before closing.
Retry the full request whenever an unfamiliar event arrives, while preserving the parser's existing strict allowlist.
Ignore unknown event types gracefully while continuing to enforce known content and lifecycle invariants.
Append the unknown event's JSON data to the active text block for later interpretation.
questions.explanation: The streaming protocol may add event types, so forward-compatible consumers should tolerate unknown events without weakening validation of recognized ones.

questions.question: A warehouse application sends a 4000-by-3000 image and asks Claude for a damaged-box bounding rectangle. Claude processes a resized image, but the application draws the returned pixel coordinates directly on the original and the box is misplaced. What is the correct remedy?
options: Switch from absolute coordinates to color names so the original renderer can infer the damaged region automatically.
Add the original image byte length to every returned coordinate before drawing the rectangle on the source.
Ask for normalized coordinates but continue interpreting each returned value as an original absolute pixel position.
Pre-resize to the model-visible dimensions or rescale the returned coordinates back to the original dimensions.
questions.explanation: The renderer and model output must share a coordinate space, achieved through one-to-one preprocessing or explicit scaling.

questions.question: A team sets a floating 'newest Sonnet' alias in shared config so everyone stays current, but two developers get diverging results on the same task the same week. Which configuration change best restores reproducibility?
options: Move the floating alias into each developer's personal user directory so a machine-local setting resolves it consistently
Add a CLAUDE.md note asking Claude to behave identically no matter which model version happens to be active that day
Raise the request's max_tokens so both developers reliably receive complete, and therefore matching, task responses
Pin an explicit, immutable model ID in the shared config so every run on every machine targets the same model version
questions.explanation: Reproducibility requires an immutable pinned model ID: a fixed version removes the drift a floating alias introduces across machines and time.

questions.question: A quality-control audit replays a prior request, but the image URL now serves a corrected photograph under the same path. The replay produces different findings. What should the system change for future audits?
options: Store only Claude's textual findings because retaining the exact image input is unnecessary after inference.
Use immutable versioned image references or retain the exact submitted bytes and their integrity hash.
Increase image resolution during replay so the newer photograph more closely approximates the original evidence.
Reuse the original prompt cache key because it permanently identifies the image returned by the URL.
questions.explanation: Versioned evidence and hashes make the multimodal input identifiable and allow a replay to use the same photograph.

questions.question: A team lead onboarding a new repository to Claude Code wants a first-draft CLAUDE.md that reflects the project's real structure and conventions instead of writing one from a blank page. Which built-in step is designed for this?
options: Run /init, which analyzes the repository and generates a starter CLAUDE.md capturing its structure and conventions for review.
Run /memory, which scans the whole repository and writes the discovered conventions directly into the persistent agent memory store.
Add a generate hook to settings.json that runs after each commit and rewrites CLAUDE.md from the current file tree automatically.
Ask for the draft while running in headless mode, since only headless mode is permitted to create files during initial project setup.
questions.explanation: Correct: /init is purpose-built to bootstrap a project's CLAUDE.md by inspecting the codebase, giving an editable first draft.

questions.question: A security-conscious team must guarantee that Claude Code never runs git push --force against the main branch, no matter how the model is prompted. Which mechanism gives a deterministic guarantee rather than a best effort?
options: Add a strongly-worded rule in CLAUDE.md forbidding force-pushes to main, since the model reliably follows clearly written instructions in its memory.
List git on the allowlist in settings.json, relying on the permission layer to automatically restrict it to safe subcommands only.
Configure a PreToolUse hook that inspects the pending command and blocks the call, because hooks are the deterministic guardrail layer.
Lower the model's temperature so that it becomes statistically incapable of ever producing the force-push command in the first place.
questions.explanation: Correct: a PreToolUse hook runs deterministic code before a tool executes and can veto the call, which is how you hard-block a specific dangerous command.

questions.question: Debugging a report of a wrong answer, an engineer replays the exact same request payload once, gets a correct answer, concludes the model is randomly flaky, and opens a transport bug. What is the sounder debugging conclusion?
options: The single successful replay proves the first failure was a dropped connection that happened to recover, so an idempotent retry-on-failure policy is the complete and sufficient fix here.
Because the output changed under an identical payload, the API must be returning cached responses that belong to other requests, so disabling prompt caching will stabilize the answer.
Default sampling makes outputs nondeterministic, so one non-reproduction proves nothing about transport; set temperature to 0 to reproduce the failure and confirm it is a model or prompt issue.
A differing answer means the underlying model ID silently changed behavior between the two calls, so pinning the request to a dated model snapshot will remove the run-to-run variation.
questions.explanation: Correct: with default sampling the model may answer differently on identical input, so a single replay cannot isolate the cause. Reducing temperature to make behavior reproducible is the right first debugging move.

questions.question: A team notices their multi-turn chat calls grow steadily more expensive as a conversation lengthens, even though each new user message is short. Given the Messages API is stateless, what is happening?
options: The SDK is holding a server-side session open between turns, and the rising cost is the idle-connection charge for keeping that session alive.
The model is silently raising its sampling temperature as the conversation lengthens, and that higher temperature is what increases the per-token price.
Each turn resends the full prior conversation as input, so input tokens -- and therefore cost -- grow with the accumulated history on every single call.
Later turns are automatically routed to a higher-priced model tier once the conversation crosses a length threshold, which raises the effective rate.
questions.explanation: Correct: a stateless API means the client re-sends the whole transcript each turn, so input cost scales with conversation length.

questions.question: A retail team is starting a product-catalog enrichment feature with moderate reasoning needs and no unusual latency pressure. An architect proposes defaulting to Opus "to be safe" on quality. What is the more disciplined starting choice?
options: Default to Opus on every call, since the highest-capability tier removes any risk of a quality shortfall showing up later in the project.
Default to Haiku on every call, because the cheapest tier is always the correct place to begin for any feature regardless of the task at hand.
Alternate randomly between all three tiers per request so the workload is spread evenly and no single tier ends up dominating the total cost.
Start on Sonnet as the balanced default, then escalate specific hard cases to Opus or drop the simplest ones to Haiku once real usage is measured.
questions.explanation: Correct: the balanced tier is the sound default, with measured escalation or de-escalation rather than pre-committing to the priciest option.

questions.question: A public-sector helpdesk handles a flood of simple FAQ lookups plus a small fraction of complex policy-interpretation cases. They want low cost without capping quality on the hard cases. Which design best fits?
options: Route every request to Opus so the hard cases are always well covered, accepting the higher per-call cost across the entire FAQ-dominated volume.
Route every request to Haiku to keep the cost as low as possible, accepting that the complex policy-interpretation cases will sometimes come back with shallow answers.
Use a cheap tier to handle and classify the bulk FAQ traffic, and escalate only the flagged complex cases to a higher-capability tier for the harder reasoning.
Send each request to all three tiers in parallel and return whichever response arrives first, balancing the cost against the latency on every single call.
questions.explanation: Correct: a tiered router spends the cheap tier on the common easy cases and reserves the expensive tier for the small hard slice.

questions.question: A manufacturing team runs a nightly job that scores tens of thousands of maintenance logs. The results are not needed until morning, and they want to cut spend. Which delivery mechanism best fits this workload?
options: Fire all the requests concurrently against the standard synchronous endpoint at full rate, since sheer parallelism across overlapping calls is what actually lowers the total token bill for the job.
Submit the work through the asynchronous Message Batches API, which processes large non-urgent volumes at a substantial per-token discount versus synchronous calls.
Enable streaming on every synchronous request, because token-by-token delivery is the mechanism that reduces the cost of a large overnight batch of calls.
Upgrade the entire job to Opus, on the theory that a more capable tier finishes each log in fewer output tokens and therefore ends up cheaper overall.
questions.explanation: Correct: a latency-tolerant overnight job is the ideal fit for the batch pathway, which trades immediacy for a meaningful cost reduction.

questions.question: A retail team caches a large stable prompt but their cache hit rate is near zero, and investigation shows they inject a fresh timestamp near the top of the system prompt on every call. What is happening?
options: Any change inside the cached prefix invalidates it, so a per-call timestamp near the top breaks the exact-match prefix and forces a full reprocess on every request.
Timestamps are stripped automatically before caching, so the near-zero hit rate must instead come from the account quietly exceeding a hidden daily cache quota it was never told about.
Cache matching ignores the system prompt and keys only on the user message, so editing the system prompt cannot possibly explain the missing cache hits the team is seeing here.
The cache matches on the total token count of the prefix alone, so as long as the overall length stays stable the injected timestamp is irrelevant and the misses have some other root cause.
questions.explanation: Correct: caching matches an exact prefix, so a changing token high in that prefix invalidates the match and defeats reuse for everything after it.

questions.question: A team wants Claude to proactively push new tokens to their server without the server issuing a request, and plans to hold open a bidirectional socket for it. What is the accurate constraint?
options: Hold open a persistent WebSocket to the Messages endpoint and the model will emit new tokens on its own whenever it has something to add, with no further request needed from the server once the socket is established.
The Messages API is request-and-response over HTTPS with optional SSE streaming of a single response, so output flows only after the app sends a request and there is no unsolicited push.
Server push works only on the higher tiers such as Opus, so upgrading the model is what enables the persistent bidirectional socket.
They must poll a status endpoint in a loop, since polling is the only way any API can deliver streamed tokens to a client.
questions.explanation: The interaction model is request/response; streaming delivers one response incrementally but the model never emits tokens unprompted.

questions.question: A manufacturing analytics team defaults every new feature to Opus "to be safe," then complains that costs are unsustainable, and a lead insists the bottleneck is always model capability. What is the more disciplined stance?
