There is no way to estimate token cost before sending a request; cost can only be known after the response returns.
questions.explanation: The dedicated count_tokens endpoint exists precisely so developers don't have to rely on rough character-ratio heuristics for pre-flight cost estimation.

questions.question: A team migrates their agentic coding assistant from an older model generation to a newer one and it begins returning 400 errors on requests that previously worked. They had been using manual extended thinking (thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}) and an assistant-turn prefill. What is the most likely explanation?
options: This reflects a documented breaking behavior change across model generations -- manual extended-thinking parameters and assistant-turn prefills are rejected on the newer generation, requiring migration to adaptive thinking and removal of the prefill pattern.
This is unrelated to the model migration; 400 errors on a previously working request always indicate an account billing issue.
The newer model generation simply has a lower rate limit, and the 400s are actually disguised rate-limit errors.
This can only be fixed by reverting to the old model permanently, since the new model has no equivalent capability.
questions.explanation: The migration guide documents exactly these two breaking changes together: manual thinking parameters and assistant-turn prefills are both rejected on the newer model generation.

questions.question: A reporting service needs Claude's reply to be a bare JSON array with no preamble, but Claude often opens with a sentence like "Here is the data:" before the array. Which Messages API technique most directly forces the response to begin at the array?
options: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening bracket so generation is constrained to continue from there, and the model cannot emit a preamble before it.
Add a system-prompt line commanding "respond with only the array and no preamble," trusting that a firm instruction removes the opening sentence.
Set a stop sequence on the opening bracket so the model halts before it, which keeps the preamble out of the returned text.
Lower the temperature to zero so the model deterministically skips the friendly opener and starts directly with the structured array content.
questions.explanation: Seeding the start of the assistant message with the opening token of the desired structure forces continuation from that point, which reliably suppresses any leading prose.

questions.domain: Input Side Vs Output Side Controls
questions.question: A team prevents secret leakage by running a regex filter over Claude's output to strip anything resembling an API key before returning it. In testing, the model still leaks a secret by describing it in plain words. What is the more robust design?
options: Expand the output regex to also match base64, hex, and spelled-out encodings so that a wider range of secret formats is caught before any response is sent to the user.
Add a system-prompt instruction that forbids Claude from ever revealing secrets, layered on top of the existing output regex to catch anything the filter happens to miss.
Stop placing the secrets in the model's context at all; keep them server-side behind a tool so there is simply nothing sensitive for the model to describe or leak.
Switch to a non-streaming response so the full text can be scanned in one pass, rather than trying to filter partial streamed chunks as they arrive incrementally.
questions.explanation: Removing the secret from context eliminates the leak at its source, which no amount of output filtering can guarantee.

questions.question: A database MCP server exposes a resources endpoint listing all tables and their schemas, intended to be read once so the agent doesn't need repeated exploratory tool calls. In practice, the agent still calls list_tables and describe_table roughly 20 times in a single session before ever referencing the resource. What is the most likely design gap?
options: Resources cannot reduce tool-call volume; only reducing the number of tables in the database itself would help.
This is expected and unavoidable; resources and tools always get used with equal frequency regardless of design.
The fix is to remove the list_tables and describe_table tools entirely, since any exploratory tool duplicating a resource's data should never exist alongside it.

The resource wasn't surfaced or described clearly enough as the preferred, one-time upfront read; resources are read-only catalogs meant to replace repeated exploratory tool calls, and the fix is ensuring the resource is discoverable and its purpose (read once at session start) is clear, rather than leaving the agent to default to incremental tool-based exploration.
questions.explanation: Resources only reduce exploratory tool calls if the agent is actually steered toward reading them first; a resource's mere existence doesn't automatically override a default pattern of incremental tool-based exploration.

questions.question: A defense supplier must run a repository-maintenance agent inside its existing Kubernetes cluster. The repository filesystem and tool execution must stay inside its controlled network, and its platform team will operate containers, credentials, and sandboxes. Which approach best fits?
options: Run the Claude Agent SDK in the supplier's infrastructure and own the surrounding isolation and operations.
Use a browser-only Claude interface and manually copy repository files into each conversation.
Use Anthropic-hosted execution solely because self-hosting always requires a custom model loop.
Replace Claude with deterministic scripts because agents cannot run inside organization-owned containers.
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK runs in a developer-operated process, allowing the organization to host the runtime near controlled files and tools.

questions.question: A developer tells a colleague, "We're using Strands for agent orchestration, so we're building on Anthropic's own agent framework." Is this an accurate characterization?
options: Yes, since Strands was designed specifically around Claude's tool-use loop and only works with Claude models.
No -- Strands Agents is an open-source SDK originally released by AWS, model-vendor-agnostic (supporting Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.), not an Anthropic-native product.
No, because Strands is published by LangChain, not AWS.
Yes, because any framework that supports Claude is considered part of Anthropic's official agent stack.
questions.explanation: Strands is explicitly multi-vendor by design and was originally released by AWS, not Anthropic -- it's a third-party abstraction layer that happens to support Claude, not an Anthropic-owned framework.

questions.question: A developer sets max_tokens to 2,000 and expects every Messages API response to contain exactly 2,000 output tokens. What does the parameter actually mean?
options: It is an output ceiling; Claude may stop earlier when the response is complete.
It is an output target; the API pads short responses until the target is reached.
It is a context limit; input and output together must always total exactly 2,000 tokens.
It is a billing minimum; the account is charged for all 2,000 tokens even if unused.
questions.explanation: max_tokens caps generated output but does not require Claude to fill the allocation when it reaches a natural endpoint.

questions.question: A public-sector team must summarize permit applications, preserve cited source locations, and route low-confidence cases to a reviewer. During implementation, how should it keep those requirements verifiable?
options: Store the requirements only in the system prompt so any generated behavior automatically counts as implementation evidence.
Map each requirement to an interface behavior, acceptance criterion, owner, and verification result through delivery.
Track only model-quality scores because functional requirements are satisfied whenever summary accuracy exceeds a single threshold.
Wait until deployment to document the final workflow because traceability before code completion creates unnecessary rework.
questions.explanation: Traceability connects business needs to implemented behavior and evidence, making omissions and changes visible across the lifecycle.

questions.domain: Software Engineering Foundations For Claude Apps
questions.question: A team is under high concurrent load and their synchronous Claude integration begins timing out on long generations. Which standard software-engineering lever, applied to their Claude integration specifically, addresses this?
options: Disable prompt caching, since cached requests are more prone to timing out under load.
Switch to the Batch API, since it is designed specifically for reducing timeouts under concurrent load.
Increase max_tokens on every request so responses complete faster.
Switch to the SDK's async client (e.g., AsyncAnthropic) combined with streaming, to fan out concurrent requests without blocking and avoid timeouts on long outputs.
questions.explanation: Async I/O plus streaming is the standard software-engineering answer to blocking timeouts under concurrent load applied specifically to the Claude SDK's async client and streaming support.

questions.question: A news app wants to show Claude's answer word-by-word as it is generated to reduce perceived latency, and a developer assumes this requires opening a bidirectional websocket. What is the correct approach?
options: Enable streaming over the standard HTTP request, which returns incremental server-sent events as tokens are produced, with no separate websocket transport required at all.
Open a persistent websocket to a dedicated realtime endpoint, since token-by-token delivery is only possible over a bidirectional socket connection maintained to the model service.
Poll the API repeatedly for partial completions, since streaming just means issuing many rapid follow-up requests and stitching the returned fragments together on the client side.
Lower the max_tokens value on each call, since shorter responses arrive sooner and progressively shrinking the output length simulates a streaming experience for the reader.
questions.explanation: Correct: streaming is delivered as server-sent events over the ordinary HTTP request, so incremental output needs no dedicated socket.

questions.question: A developer needs an extraction endpoint to be output-consistent for every call and decides to add ten <example> input-output pairs to the system prompt, believing "more examples always improve consistency." What consideration is missing from this reasoning?
options: Few-shot/multishot prompting is documented as effective with "a few well-crafted examples," and while examples generally help output consistency, the core lesson is that a large, poorly-curated example set adds token cost and can dilute focus without addressing whether the underlying task even needs multishot at all versus a schema-level fix.
Few-shot examples never improve consistency; only structured output schemas can guarantee consistent formatting.
Ten examples is the documented minimum threshold below which multishot prompting has no effect at all.
Adding examples only helps if they are wrapped in Markdown bold text rather than plain prose.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance specifically recommends a FEW well-crafted examples, not an unbounded count; quality and fit to the actual failure mode matter more than raw quantity.

questions.question: An agent compacts earlier turns into a prose paragraph to save tokens. Later it needs an exact order ID and a dollar figure that were mentioned early on, but the summary rounded the figure and dropped the ID. What compaction principle was violated?
options: Compaction should hand the summarization to a larger model tier, on the assumption that a stronger summarizer would not have dropped the identifier or rounded the figure.
Compaction should be deferred until the very last possible turn so that the maximum amount of original detail is retained in the window for as long as it can be.
Compaction should always keep the full original turns and never summarize, because any summarization inevitably risks discarding some potentially useful detail later.
Compaction should preserve load-bearing identifiers and exact values verbatim in a structured facts block, summarizing only the narrative around them, not the data itself.
questions.explanation: Compaction is safe only when critical data -- IDs, amounts, dates -- is carried forward verbatim in a structured block; prose summarization is fine for narrative but must never round or drop the values later steps depend on.

questions.question: A healthcare agent reads patient-uploaded documents (untrusted), has access to the full patient-record database (private data), and can call a generic http_post tool. A reviewer flags this combination as especially dangerous. Which principle names the risk and its fix?
options: The dangerous pattern is private-data access combined with exposure to untrusted content and an external-send capability; break it by removing one leg, such as the http_post tool.
The risk is context-window exhaustion from large patient documents; the fix is to summarize each upload before it is added to the record context on every turn.
The risk is that Opus-class reasoning over medical text may hallucinate diagnoses; the fix is a lower-temperature Haiku model dedicated to the extraction task.
The risk is a missing prompt cache on the patient record; the fix is a stable cached prefix that keeps the private data immutable across the agent's requests.
questions.explanation: When all three capabilities coexist, an injection can read private data and send it out; eliminating any one leg neutralizes the exfiltration path.

questions.question: A developer needs a single, one-off internal function -- "look up a customer's loyalty tier by ID" against a private, internal database used only by their own team's agent -- and defaults to standing up a full MCP server for it, reasoning "MCP is always the most powerful and most correct choice." Evaluate this reasoning.
options: This reasoning is correct, but only because internal databases specifically require MCP servers and cannot be accessed via custom tools at all.
This reasoning is correct; MCP servers should always be the default choice regardless of scope, since more governance is never a downside.

This over-invests in governance and latency overhead for a narrow, single-team, single-use case; a custom tool (defined directly via the Agent SDK's in-process mechanism) is the better fit here, since MCP's centralized-governance and reusability benefits aren't needed when there's no cross-team reuse or multi-system integration to manage.
This is incorrect, but the actual better choice is a built-in tool, since built-in tools can be extended to query any private database.
questions.explanation: The exam's core lesson is matching mechanism overhead to actual reuse and governance need; a narrow single-team lookup doesn't need MCP's centralized governance and is better served by a lighter-weight custom tool.
